statement: A passenger sits by the window of a train travelling at 70 km/h. A train 150 m long passes in the opposite direction, taking exactly 6 seconds from the moment its front reaches her window until its back passes it. What is the speed of the other train, in km/h?

choices.misconception: I worked out 150 ÷ 6 = 25 metres per second and forgot both to change it into km/h and to take away the speed of her own train.
I thought the two trains share the closing speed of 90 km/h equally, so each has half of it.
I found the closing speed of the two trains, 90 km/h, and forgot to take away the speed of her own train.
I added the 70 km/h of her own train to the closing speed of 90 km/h instead of subtracting it.

hints: How fast does the other train move past her window, in metres per second?

From her seat, the other train goes past at the two speeds added, because the trains move in opposite directions. Find that closing speed from the length and the time, change it to km/h, then remove her own speed.
The other train moves 150 m past her in 6 seconds: 25 metres per second, which is 90 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Relative to the passenger, the other train moves its own length, 150 m, in 6 seconds, so the closing speed is 25 metres per second. One metre per second is 3.6 km/h, so this is 25 × 3.6 = 90 km/h. The trains move in opposite directions, so the closing speed is the sum of their speeds: 70 + v = 90, which gives v = 20 km/h. The transferable idea: in passing problems, use the speed of one object relative to the other, and remember that opposite directions add.

whyOnTest: Passing questions test relative speed and unit changes together: closing speed from length and time, then convert and subtract.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
